questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The degree-drop rule
questions.learningObjective: explain why a constant row certifies the degree of a rule exactly
questions.stem: Explain why a cost rule of degree d always produces a constant row at position d in a difference table, and why that row certifies the degree exactly rather than merely an upper bound.

answer.exemplar: Differencing a polynomial of degree d multiplies the leading term by d and produces a rule of degree d minus 1, because the two leading terms cancel in (n plus 1) minus n. Repeating that d times leaves a constant, and one more differencing step turns that constant into zeros. Since the row at position d is a non-zero constant rather than a linear row, no rule of higher degree could have produced the table, so the degree is exactly d and not merely at most d. The value of that constant is a times d factorial, which also recovers the leading coefficient of the rule.

questions.explanation: A strong answer mentions that leading terms cancel at each differencing step, that the constant at row d equals a times d factorial, and that a non-zero constant rules out a higher degree.
questions.hint: Watch the leading terms cancel at each differencing step.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Differences of a geometric list
questions.learningObjective: explain why a difference table cannot extrapolate a geometric costing list
questions.stem: Explain why a difference table cannot be used to extrapolate a geometric costing list the way it extrapolates a quadratic one.

answer.exemplar: A difference table extends a list only when some row becomes constant, because a constant row is what lets you carry the pattern forward one step at a time. In a geometric list every row is the row above multiplied by the same ratio, so no row is ever constant and there is no constant to carry. A student who tries anyway ends up adding a constant difference to a list that is really multiplying, which produces a straight line where the truth curves upward. The fix is to look for a ratio in the first row rather than a constant, and to extend by multiplying instead of adding.

questions.explanation: A good answer says a table extends a list only when a row is constant, that a geometric list keeps a ratio instead, and that adding a constant difference to a multiplying list is the error.
questions.hint: Extending a table needs a constant row to carry forward.

questions.stem: Explain why the difference table of the triangular numbers has a constant second difference of 1.

answer.exemplar: The triangular numbers count the total of the first n natural numbers, so going from n to n plus 1 adds exactly n plus 1 items to the pile. The counting argument and the table therefore say the same thing.
